abstract: Modern program evaluation prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) because prior research found that observational estimates of program impacts often diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks. We revisit this finding --- which was based on small survey datasets --- in the era of large-scale administrative data. Using anonymized income tax records covering all American adults between 1999 and 2025, we estimate the effects of workforce training programs on earnings by using machine learning models to predict counterfactuals from rich data on prior work histories, demographics, and residential locations. Rather than testing whether our observational estimates are unbiased, we use 37 RCTs to estimate the distribution of their bias. We find that our machine learning estimates closely match the RCT estimates, with root mean squared error (RMSE) comparable to that of the RCTs themselves. Our method reduces RMSE by 60% relative to parametric estimators used in prior work because our larger samples and richer covariates permit more flexible, higher-dimensional models of the counterfactual. Applying our method to a broader set of sites and enrollment years beyond the experimental sample, we find that treatment effects on earnings vary substantially across locations and over time, even within a given program. Programs that place more participants into target-sector jobs generate the largest earnings gains, with impacts that persist even after participants leave their initial jobs. These findings provide guidance for improving job training programs and, more broadly, illustrate a scalable approach to program evaluation that uses observational data to construct experimentally validated ``digital twins.''

abstract: Generative AI tools for research are widely deployed, yet individual productivity gains do not guarantee better team research. We argue that how AI use is structured matters alongside access. Personal AI tools may amplify two failures under deadline pressure: a consumption bottleneck, in which generation outpaces team-visible evaluation, and AI-induced research silos, in which private human-AI loops displace shared decision-making. We motivate this position with a mechanism-generating pilot: a 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three independently operating teams, within a seventeen-person session. Both patterns recurred across teams and evidence sources. Of 33 logged AI interactions, one was accepted outright and 27 lacked a recorded disposition; missing records alone do not establish absent evaluation. A parallel autonomous pipeline produced a complete draft without in-session human evaluation, illustrating production capacity rather than comparative quality. We propose Human-AI-Human collaboration: an interaction topology in which AI connects researchers' contexts and supports inspectable collective evaluation and decision-making. The pilot does not isolate AI-specific effects from time pressure or workflow practices. abstract: Frontier AI labs compete in a contest for commercial leadership while sharing the risk of catastrophe. Each lab gains from arriving earlier but bears only part of the hazard its speed adds, which this paper calls the hazard externality. In an illustrative calibrated takeoff model, three racing labs get through the takeoff period in 18 months, while a common rule on research shares would stretch it to 69 months. Neither force alone explains racing that fast. Removing the contest first closes over ninety percent of the gap in catastrophe probability between racing and a common rule when the catastrophe probability at full speed is 75 percent, and 69 percent when it is 25 percent; averaged over both orders of removal, the contest explains 65 and 44 percent. More labs make each lab race harder, when industry hazard at a common research share does not depend on the number of labs. Under open source in its ideal form, where every lab publishes its capability findings at once, labs slow to the coordinated pace, because no lab can get ahead and each bears all the hazard its research adds. One lab's restraint achieves much less than a common rule. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence of September 2026 audits safety but sets no limit on speed. In the model it does not slow the race, because each lab still gains as much from speeding up.

abstract: Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.

abstract: Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities. Trust is frequently invoked to explain creativity, exploration, and opportunity formation, yet remains theorized through predictability and evaluability, which entrepreneurial opportunities often lack ex ante. We distinguish three forms of vulnerability acceptance: uncertainty creating, releasing, and decreasing trust. Each transforms the uncertainty it engages, which in turn reinforces or unsettles that form, so no form is terminal. Their salience shifts across opportunity formation, interpretive recombination, and realization, and misalignment between a form and the conditions it confronts impairs entrepreneurial progress. Trust thereby becomes a means through which epistemic conditions are produced, not only a response to them. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurship exposes forms of vulnerability that cannot be explained by risk‐based models of trust alone. Entrepreneurs often face the practical question: “Trust them to do what?” The answer depends on the kind of agency they are willing to be vulnerable to, and it changes as an opportunity takes shape. That may mean backing people to take the work somewhere no one can yet specify, relying on others' expertise to make sense of what is emerging, or counting on them to deliver what was agreed. Trust is therefore not only a way of reducing uncertainty but a means of transforming it, and progress depends on recognizing when the prevailing form fits the conditions and when it does not.

abstract: Research Summary We replicate and extend Flammer's (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility. Flammer found that investors react positively to eco‐friendly events and negatively to eco‐harmful events, with positive reactions diminishing and negative reactions intensifying from 1980 to 2009. We confirm her results in a narrow replication and find that these time trends persist in a quasi‐replication extending the sample through 2019, despite major shifts in the institutional environment for sustainability investing. We then extend Flammer by incorporating financial materiality and find that the investor reactions and time trends Flammer observed are primarily concentrated in material events. Notably, investors drew this distinction throughout the 40‐year window we study, predating the institutionalization of materiality‐based sustainability analysis. Managerial Summary We examine how investors respond to companies' environmental actions. Analyzing 40 years of data on US‐listed public firms, we find that investors reward companies for eco‐friendly actions and penalize them for harmful ones. Over time, these reactions have shifted: investors have grown less enthusiastic about eco‐friendly actions and more critical of harmful ones. Importantly, investors react primarily to environmental actions that are financially relevant, or “material,” to the business and were doing so well before formal standards existed. Within material actions, positive reactions to eco‐friendly initiatives have weakened while negative reactions to eco‐harmful ones have grown stronger. These findings suggest that managers should prioritize environmental initiatives closely tied to their company's financial performance.

abstract: Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

abstract: This paper investigates whether local institutional quality is associated with firm-level innovation from an economic geography perspective. Focusing on Italian manufacturing firms, we examine whether cross-province differences in institutional quality are related to firms’ patenting activity and whether this relationship varies by firm size. Drawing on a longitudinal dataset of more than 125,000 manufacturing firms observed from 2011 to 2019, we combine firm-level patent data with a province-level measure of institutional quality. Our results show that higher local institutional quality is positively associated with firms’ patenting activity. Moreover, the relationship varies across firms and institutional dimensions, as improvements in control of corruption, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, and voice and accountability are associated with larger increases in patenting among smaller firms. By contrast, we find no evidence that the association between the rule-of-law dimension and patenting varies by firm size.

abstract: A substantial literature explores workers’ transitions into entrepreneurial business ownership, while freelance, on-demand self-employment, a distinct and increasingly prevalent mode of labour market participation, remains comparatively understudied. Using an original large survey conducted in 16 countries, we investigate the determinants of workers’ intentions to leave their main salaried job to engage in freelance, on-demand self-employment. We find that socio-demographic characteristics, job conditions, and behavioural traits are systematically associated with these intentions, though several patterns diverge from those documented in the entrepreneurship literature. A detailed heterogeneity analysis substantiates variation across occupations, task types, and individual characteristics. Workers in more vulnerable positions exhibit higher intentions to transition into freelance, on-demand self-employment, a form of work often associated with lower protection and higher income risk.

abstract: Management scholars have recently started to disentangle how the social-class background of top executives influences firms’ strategic outcomes. Using a large sample of German CEOs, we explore the role that economic and cultural resources available during childhood play in fostering firm growth, both individually and in combination. Our analyses reveal that the economic and cultural resources marking a CEO’s social-class origin relate to firm growth in complex ways. While both are positively associated with firm growth, their relative importance differs across growth measures, and their interaction is negatively related to sales and total asset growth. Contour plot analyses attribute lower growth rates particularly to firms led by CEOs who grew up with either low or high combinations of economic and cultural resources. Additional analyses show that these relationships differ within the CEO group depending on CEOs’ own educational attainment, pointing to mobility-related heterogeneity in how class origin translates into firm growth. Besides highlighting the relevance of imprinting, our exploratory study emphasizes the importance of disentangling social subclasses within the CEO group and their impact on different growth types.

abstract: By strategically leveraging public procurement, governments can harness market competition to drive business innovation and sustainable development. It remains unclear, however, how this premise is affected by heightened security awareness due to increasing geopolitical tensions. Focusing on European Union (EU) member states, we examine how security-oriented practices in public procurement affect tender outcomes. Using data from a recent pan-European survey of 1613 procurement projects, coupled with data from the EU's tender platform Tender Electronic Daily, we test the effect of using national security assessments (NSAs) during tender preparation on competition, innovation, sustainability, and critical technology procurement. We find that conducting such assessments has positive effects on innovation and on critical technology procurement, but only for tenders won by domestic suppliers. NSAs can thus create urgency and mobilize resources to innovate through public procurement, but possibly in a way that reinforces national rather than EU-wide technological development. We identify a tension between the need for research and coordination of NSA development at the EU level to avoid market distortions arising from uncontrolled NSA proliferation versus a heightened bureaucratic burden for suppliers. We also argue that stimulating joint cross-border innovation procurement, particularly of critical technologies, is key to fully leveraging the benefits of the EU internal market when pursuing strategic policy goals.

abstract: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1-4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an 'add-on' architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

abstract: More than 65 years after the Brown v. Board of Education ruling that school segregation is unconstitutional, public schools across the United States are again experiencing rising segregation. In districts like San Francisco, efforts to implement district-wide choice policies have largely failed to reverse these trends. Since 2019, we have collaborated with the San Francisco Unified School District to design a student assignment policy meeting the district’s goals of diversity, predictability, and proximity. We use optimization techniques to develop policies restricting choice to zones. We compare these to district-wide choice policies by estimating a choice model using historical application data and simulating assignment. Our results show multiple policies can reduce school segregation while preserving varying degrees of proximity, choice, and predictability. Zone-based policies with reserves reduce the concentration of racial minority students in high-poverty schools and maintain proximity, but reduce choice. District-wide choice with reserves and distance-based priority can further reduce segregation, but at the cost of predictability. Tradeoffs are necessary as no policy dominates another policy. In addition, we show that spatial segregation indices capture average patterns in these tradeoffs but miss important variation revealed by our simulation framework. Our work informed the design and approval of a zone-based policy in San Francisco in 2020, and supports ongoing policy implementation.

abstract: Human social networks involve multiple kinds of relationships—such as friendship, health support, and economic exchange—that serve different functions and compete for limited time and resources. Here, we deploy a compositional framework to infer functional roles in directed multiplex networks. We distinguish outgoing ties that reflect social behavior of individuals’ allocation of social effort from incoming ties that capture structural dependence, or social appeal. The method accounts for heterogeneity in individual activity levels and layer density across relational domains. Applying this approach to multiplex sociocentric network data from 23,378 individuals across 176 rural Honduran villages, we uncover well-defined role structures spanning friendship, health-related support, and economic interactions. We find a pronounced asymmetry: behavioral (outgoing) roles exhibit weaker demographic association but stronger geographic organization than incoming roles. This is consistent with shared local environments at the village-wide level shaping social action. In contrast, structural (incoming) roles show more pronounced life-course transitions and socioeconomic differentiation, with little geographic association. Taken together, these patterns reveal a systematic difference in how social behavior and social appeal are organized in multiplex social systems. This approach illustrates a general framework for studying social roles, inequality, and life-course dynamics in complex social systems.

abstract: Reports of parents’ names in Social Security Application records allow us to quantify at a population level the extent and nature of historical last name changes by immigrants. Our analysis of European, Middle Eastern, and Asian immigrants of the early to mid-20th-century finds that more than 80% kept their last names. Computational linguistic analysis shows that most of those who did change preserved their surname’s ethnic signal, leaving only about 5% of all immigrants trying to disguise their foreign origins. Of these, Jewish immigrants had the highest rate of ethnicity-concealing last name changes; Italian, Japanese, and Chinese immigrants all had the lowest. Our proposed framework helps understand the variation: name changes were rarest where ethnic community networks were densest and where passing as unmarked was least credible—as among visibly non-White immigrants. Our findings challenge the dominant assimilationist narrative that immigrants in this era had to shed their foreign identities to enter the American mainstream. “Becoming White” by adopting an English surname was not a large part of historical immigrant experience. Rather, the overwhelming majority of immigrants chose to openly preserve their ethnic origins. Our results also suggest that nominal record linkage of historical immigrant populations may be more feasible than previously assumed.

abstract: This paper uses newly harmonized survey and register data on incomes and labor market outcomes as the basis for consistent comparisons of inequalities across 17 North American and European countries over the period 1995–2021. We examine trends in disposable income inequality in the working-age population, defined as persons aged 25 to 60, as well as its component parts of market income inequality and redistribution through government tax and transfer systems. We adjust incomes to allow for changes in education, population aging, and household structure in each country. We test for convergence across countries in demographically-adjusted disposable income inequality, along with market income inequality and redistribution. There is strong evidence of convergence over time in disposable income inequality across the 17 countries, despite a divergence in the dispersion of market income inequality driven by very heterogeneous trends for hours of work and the number of workers in households across countries. Consistent with this we find a strong convergence across countries in the dispersion of our measure of redistribution. There are reductions over time in inequality-reducing redistribution in the Nordic countries and increases in some other European and North American countries, with the net effect being more similarity across countries, a lower average level of redistribution, and a higher average level of disposable income inequality. These trends are being driven by the bottom 95% of the income distribution. Our results are robust to a variety of alternative specifications including the measure of inequality, trimming of data outliers, and sample period.

abstract: Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

abstract: Workplace authority is a key individual and organizational resource to which women typically have more limited access than men. Yet, less is known about how parenthood shapes this gender disparity and how the relationship varies across employment regimes. Drawing on nationally representative, longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022), I examine within-person changes in women’s and men’s access to supervisory authority following parenthood, with particular attention to variation across the state and private sectors. Fixed-effects results show that, overall, women’s likelihood of holding authority declines after becoming mothers, especially after having two or more children, whereas men experience little change. These dynamics differ by work sector. A considerable motherhood penalty is concentrated in the private sector, whereas a fatherhood premium emerges only in the state sector. Parenthood therefore widens the gender gap in authority in both sectors through distinct patterns. These findings suggest that employment regimes condition the gendered meanings of parenthood and how they translate into access to authority. In China, the state sector’s formal protections may buffer motherhood-related disadvantages, whereas its male-dominated hierarchy and pronatalist agendas may sustain fatherhood-related rewards.

abstract: This study maps the division of music in China and examines the mechanisms underlying its formation. Methodologically, it introduces multidimensional item response theory (MIRT), a latent-trait approach rarely used in cultural sociology, to identify the social divisions of taste before examining their social stratification through regression analysis. The findings reveal six taste profiles: high-status traditional music; pop music stratified into middlebrow Hong Kong and Taiwan classics, unstratified mainstream Chinese pop, and low-status local music; and foreign music divided into high-status selective forms and unstratified trendy foreign pop. These divisions do not cleanly align with genre categories, a highbrow–lowbrow hierarchy, or omnivore–univore patterns in established accounts. Instead, they reveal dual forms of high-status taste—state-consecrated heritage and cosmopolitan selective foreign pop—reflecting a multidimensional structure organized around region of origin, historical prestige, cohort, and popularity. More broadly, this study reveals how cultural stratification in China extends beyond Bourdieusian models centered on domestic field competition to encompass global flows, state-directed legitimation, and historical local trajectories. These findings extend theories of cultural distinction beyond the assumptions derived from dominant Western liberal-market societies and offer a framework for understanding how cultural hierarchies are constituted across wider national contexts.

abstract: Prior research views cash holdings, or high‐discretionary slack, as a buffer against shocks or a catalyst for strategic change. Drawing on stakeholder salience theory, we argue that cash can also reshape managers' interpretation and prioritization of employee hiring‐related claims, thereby increasing hiring, and that this effect is more pronounced when structural influences heighten the salience of those claims. Study 1, a large‐scale field study of Belgian firms, finds a positive but diminishing relationship between cash and hiring. This relationship strengthens under conditions of greater firm dependence on specific employee groups or following an exogenous legal reform, both of which are hypothesized to make the salience of specific employee groups more apparent. In Study 2, a vignette experiment offers causal support for the hypothesized mechanism, with employee salience cues strengthening how managers translate cash into hiring allocations. Combined, our findings contribute to research on slack resources and stakeholder salience by showing that managers use high‐discretionary cash not only for buffering or strategic change but also to respond to salient stakeholders.

abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

abstract: Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

abstract: The contemporary social sciences are seeing a resurgence of interest in social class, prompted by widening economic inequalities. While much research associated with this resurgence remains true to the core maxims of class analysis, it has yet to fully grapple with contemporary transformations in class structure. In advanced economies such as Australia, the combined effects of wage stagnation and asset price inflation, supported by pro-asset owner policy regimes, have made asset ownership increasingly central to life chances. In this article, we explore whether the rise in asset-based inequalities is effecting a change in subjective social class identities. We ask: who identifies as working or middle class? And, have the determinants of social class identification changed over time? To investigate these questions, we analyse the series of Australian Election Study surveys fielded from 1987 to 2022, focusing on the period since 2001. By examining change in the determinants of social class identity over time, we show that homeownership has become an increasingly important factor shaping identification with the middle class, while renters are becoming more likely to identify as working class. While asset ownership has become increasingly important for class identities, the impact of more traditional indicators of class, including education and supervisory roles at work, has weakened over time. This article therefore demonstrates how asset ownership is transforming social class identities.

abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

abstract: The advance of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has enabled chatbots to be emotionally responsive. In customer service, expressing empathy is a critical component of employee emotional responsiveness and a popular recovery strategy following service failure. However, the impact of empathy expressed by a chatbot is less clear. In this research, we investigate how and why chatbot-expressed empathy after service failure may influence customers’ service evaluations differently. Extending the psychological reactance literature, we propose that an empathetic chatbot may trigger customer reactance due to the unique nature of AI chatbots (vs. humans). We further propose that the triggered reactance can undermine perceptions of a chatbot’s competence and warmth, ultimately hurting service evaluations. We conducted three laboratory experiments to test these predictions. Our theoretical framework and findings illuminate the more nuanced and distinct role of empathy expressed by AI chatbots, and they suggest a critical need for chatbot developers and companies deploying chatbots to be aware of user reactance in customer service.

abstract: Importance: Most children living with noncitizen adults are US citizens and eligible for safety-net programs that support their health and development. Intensified immigration enforcement and proposed restrictions in 2025 may have deterred enrollment, but national estimates for children are lacking. Objective: To determine whether safety-net participation declined among children in noncitizen families in 2025, relative to children in naturalized-citizen families. Design: Repeated cross-sectional study with a difference-in-differences design using the 2022-2025 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), comparing 2025 with 2022-2024. Setting: Nationally representative survey of US households. Participants: Of 29,565 sample children (ages 0-17), 24,479 met inclusion criteria. The analysis compared 3,098 children in noncitizen families with 2,733 in naturalized-citizen families. Exposure: Living in a noncitizen family (sample adult not a US citizen) vs a naturalized-citizen family (sample adult a naturalized citizen) in 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures: Medicaid or Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) coverage at interview; Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), free or reduced-price school meal (ages 5-17), and Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) receipt in the past 12 months. Results: The 5,831 children had a weighted mean age of 9.0 years (47.2% female; 53.8% Hispanic). Of children in noncitizen families, 74.3% were US citizens. In adjusted models, relative to children in naturalized-citizen families, Medicaid or CHIP coverage among children in noncitizen families declined by 7.4 percentage points (95% CI, −14.3 to −0.5), SNAP receipt by 6.4 points (95% CI, −12.8 to −0.03), and school meal receipt by 8.2 points (95% CI, −16.1 to −0.2). WIC receipt did not change significantly (0.1 points; 95% CI, −5.9 to 6.1). There were no differential pre-trends, and declines were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance: In this repeated cross-sectional national study, safety-net participation among children in noncitizen families, most of whom were US citizens, declined in 2025 relative to children in naturalized-citizen families, before eligibility restrictions took effect. Reduced health coverage and nutrition assistance during childhood may have lasting consequences for health and development. Outreach and protections for enrollee data may help keep eligible children enrolled.

In both studies, higher prayer frequency strongly predicted lower social progress. abstract: This article addresses Roger Casement’s use of ethnographic fieldwork during his investigation in the Putumayo region of the Upper Amazon. It explores three interpretations of Casement’s humanitarianism: emotional, colonial, and as indicative of a lifelong commitment to Indigenous rights. The article examines his accounts of advocacy for Indigenous Amazonians, including practical aid, the amplification of their voices and support for armed resistance, and concludes that these demonstrate a commitment to Indigenous rights. Casement’s fieldwork methodology is explored in terms of his effective use of the ethnographic methods of the time and his anticipation of Spradley’s mid-twentieth-century ethnographic approaches. Casement’s statement of his methodology, thorough descriptions, intensive interviews, external corroboration, and maintenance of a fieldwork journal can all be compared with Spradley’s interpretation of ethnography. These interpretations are reinforced by Casement’s interviews with Barbadian overseers, in which he overcomes barriers of ethnicity and class, demonstrating both skilled ethnographic fieldwork and a non-racist approach. His investigation and ethnographic writing meet the twin purposes of ethnography: furthering our understanding of the Indigenous peoples of the Amazon and serving the interests of humankind by exposing the crimes against humanity in the Putumayo.

abstract: When do family roles and economic interests shape political choice? Married women outside the labor force have become a reference point in American political discourse since 2016, yet whether they vote differently from married women in paid work, once their backgrounds are considered, has not been examined with contemporary data. Using the Cooperative Election Study for 2016, 2020 and 2024 (15,633 married women aged 25-60, of whom 4,122 identified as homemakers), we estimated the difference in Republican presidential vote between homemakers and employed married women, adjusting for age, race and education and, in supplemental analyses, for family income, children and religion. Homemakers were 5.9 percentage points more likely to vote Republican across the pooled elections after adjustment (3.5 points after further adjustment). The gap was 2.8 points in 2016, 4.9 in 2020 and 10.3 in 2024, and in 2024 it was concentrated almost entirely among mothers, at 11.9 points against 1.1 among women without a child at home. Demographic characteristics fixed before labor-force exit accounted for most of the unadjusted difference and partisanship for the remainder. Three further results bear on this interpretation. First, married men outside the labor force leaned in the opposite direction. Second, homemakers differed from employed wives on gender-role attitudes but not on abortion, moral traditionalism or affect toward the Republican party. Third, longitudinal 2020-2024 data showed negligible vote switching among women already at home. Homemakers were 12 points less likely to be validated voters in 2024 but this was fully accounted for by demographics, and non-voting homemakers were at least as Republican in intention as those who voted. The gap was more closely associated with beliefs about family and gender roles than with economic position. This is notable because policies supporting women's economic security, health and family well-being have in recent decades been more strongly associated with the Democratic platform. The findings suggest that homemakers and employed wives may place different weight on economic independence, family structure and other dimensions of family well-being when making political choices, challenging the idea that women vote as a unified political bloc.

abstract: This article examines how users of Cebulka, the largest Polish-language darknet drug cryptomarket, construct and negotiate their online identities. Utilizing nineteen in-depth interviews with vendors and buyers, the research employs a qualitative methodology informed by reflexive thematic analysis, social identity theory, the SIDE model. Based on the data, five themes are developed: 1) lower perceived physical and social danger; 2) greater knowledge, technical competence, and access to higher-quality products; 3) care for others; 4) higher social status; and 5) separation between darknet personas and offline lives. Across these themes, Cebulka’s users collectively framed themselves as an elite community distinct from street-level market participants. Thus the cryptomarket operates not just as a transactional space but as a site of identity work and symbolic boundary drawing—one that inverts the context collapse and algorithmic datafication typical of the visible web. These findings carry implications for harm reduction, drug policy, and the sociology of online communities, while highlighting the ambivalent, exclusionary character of the market’s technical barriers.

abstract: Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 3, spanning roughly 60–30 ka, was a period of climatic volatility and demographic change worldwide, yet in southern Africa its archaeology has remained comparatively overlooked. Building on Peter Mitchell’s 2008 call for renewed engagement with this period, this review considers how new dates, analyses, and approaches have begun to transform our understanding of MIS 3 occupation, at the end of the Middle Stone Age. Developments in radiocarbon and luminescence dating, re-excavation of legacy sites, and regionally focused studies are closing key chronological and spatial gaps, revealing a more complex picture of human settlement and behaviour. MIS 3—its climate, archaeology, and the research paradigms that surround it —is set into context by also considering the Howiesons Poort and Early Later Stone Age periods that frame it. A biome-scale synthesis highlights both progress and persisting gaps, offering an updated view of MIS 3 as a period of marked ecological and behavioural diversity within the subcontinent’s later Pleistocene prehistory.

abstract: Research on conversational AI and politics has largely examined two directions of influence separately: how AI shapes citizens’ political attitudes and judgement, and how users’ characteristics and self-presentation shape the responses AI gives them. This article theorises how the two become coupled through epistemic efficacy, a person’s perceived capacity to understand an issue, weigh the evidence and reach a judgement of their own. How capable users present themselves as being may condition the assistance they receive, and that assistance may in turn update how capable they feel, conditioning the next interaction. The central distinction is between assistance that scaffolds political judgement, supporting users as they evaluate evidence and trade-offs for themselves, and assistance that substitutes for it, performing that evaluative work on their behalf. Drawing on an account of epistemic autonomy as governed dependence, the article treats neither as inherently good or bad and assesses assistance by whether it leaves users meaningful control over their judgement. Scaffolding may build confidence in line with the judgement users exercise, whereas substitution may increase reliance and, particularly when combined with validation of the user, raise confidence beyond competence. The article separates efficacy from attitude certainty, explains why AI conclusions differ from conventional political cues, and states falsifiable propositions for each link of the loop. The resulting dynamics have implications for epistemic autonomy and for democratic inequality, because citizens may differ in whether the assistance they receive leaves political judgement in their own hands.

abstract: Do schools reduce or amplify learning gaps by socioeconomic background? I develop a formal model that clarifies the estimands implicit in the literature and synthesizes its seemingly contradictory findings by distinguishing between exposure, or how much schooling children receive, and quality, or which schools they attend. The model shows that schools can compensate for inequality, by displacing more unequal learning outside school, while simultaneously reproducing it, both positionally, through the sorting of children into schools of unequal quality, and dispositionally, through differences in how children convert schooling into learning. Empirically, I test three of the model's predictions using Danish register data and variation from changes in school district boundaries over time. I find that the effects of school quality exceed those of exposure, are concentrated among socioeconomically disadvantaged children, and are larger where sorting into schools is stronger. Equalizing school quality can therefore be an effective means of reducing learning inequalities.

abstract: Emergency responder communications failures have long posed challenges to interagency coordination, prompting nationwide efforts to improve interoperability following the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. However, the extent to which regional initiatives have addressed persistent communications barriers remains an important question. This study evaluates the efficacy of regional firefighter communications systems in Los Angeles County, California, focusing on the Los Angeles Regional Interoperable Communications System (LARICS) and the Interagency Communications Interoperability System (ICI). Its purpose is to examine how these initiatives support interdepartmental coordination and identify what limitations, experienced during 9/11, continue into the present day. The study employed a two-phase qualitative approach grounded in first responder perspectives. Phase I consisted of open-ended interviews with four personnel across three Los Angeles County fire departments, including two field personnel and two communications personnel. Phase II used a five-point Likert scale to assess participants’ perceptions of communications technology, its development over their careers, and the relative influence of technological and procedural factors on communications challenges. Findings indicate that regional interoperability initiatives have supported interdepartmental coordination and provided redundant communications channels. Interviewees generally reported improvements in communications technology over their careers and satisfaction with existing systems, while also identifying continuing needs for improvement. Persistent barriers include radio signal attenuation inside buildings, incompatible technologies and frequencies, and differences in agency terminology and procedures. Participants did not consistently attribute communications problems primarily to technological limitations, underscoring the importance of organizational practices alongside equipment. Although the small, nonrandom interview sample limits generalizability, the findings suggest that regional initiatives have improved communications capabilities without fully resolving the operational challenges facing firefighters.

abstract: International students' host-language use and social integration are usually explained by proficiency or national origin. This study argues that host-world affiliation is produced by contact infrastructure: the repeated, low-stakes occasions for contact that institutions and living arrangements provide. A wall of host reticence, produced by both sides, bounds it. The COVID-era withdrawal of these occasions is read as a revelatory rupture that made them visible by removing them. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design drew on a survey of international students (N = 176) and 39 interviews with 40 international students at one national research university in Japan. Four domestic students were interviewed as a labelled host-side comparison. Choice of the Japanese survey form indexed host-language orientation. Origin dominated that choice, while contact-type indicators were weak. The interviews explain the pattern. Affiliation followed the occasions for contact. When the pandemic removed them, reported loss largely tracked how much a student's world had rested on them. One of the 40 cases ran against this. Host and international students placed the campus boundary in the same location: in reticence and missing shared ground, not hostility. Participants described the wider society, by contrast, as hostile through housing, policing, and hiring. Nationality worked as a marker read from outside, not as a driver of conduct. The lever for belonging is the design of contact occasions, not language instruction alone.

abstract: Traditional conflict resolution remains an important component of local peace governance in many Nigerian communities, yet its contemporary operation cannot be understood solely through claims of cultural legitimacy or accessibility. This study examines how the Otaru-in-Council functions as a local peacebuilding institution in Auchi, Edo State, with attention to its mechanisms, perceived contributions, inclusionary limits and interaction with formal justice institutions. The study examines the structure and functions of the Otaru-in-Council, identifies the conflict resolution mechanisms employed, assesses their perceived advantages and challenges, and considers conditions for constructive interaction between traditional and formal justice systems. A qualitative case study design was adopted. Primary evidence was obtained through in-depth semi-structured interviews with 30 purposively selected participants comprising traditional rulers and palace officials, senior chiefs and elders, ward and quarter heads, youth representatives, women representatives, civil society actors and community residents. Two non-participant observations of open dispute-resolution sessions and documentary materials supplemented the interviews. Data were analysed thematically, with triangulation, member checking and thick description used to strengthen trustworthiness. Mediation, reconciliation rituals, adjudication, consensus-building and arbitration were reported as principal mechanisms. Participants associated the traditional institution with cultural legitimacy, relatively low cost, accessibility, speed and restoration of social relations. At the same time, respondents reported gender exclusion, weak documentation, political interference, elite bias, limited enforcement capacity and tensions with formal law. The findings suggest that the contribution of the Otaru-in-Council to local peacebuilding is conditioned by both legitimacy and institutional safeguards. The Otaru-in-Council should be understood neither as a substitute for the state justice system nor as an inherently effective institution. Its peacebuilding significance lies in its embeddedness in local social relations and its capacity to convene disputants, while its limitations arise partly from exclusion, politicisation and uncertain interfaces with formal law. Reforms should clarify referral and jurisdictional boundaries, strengthen documentation, widen women’s and youth participation, develop human-rights and procedural capacity, and establish practical coordination between customary and formal institutions without eroding the authority that makes local mechanisms socially meaningful.

abstract: A growing body of sociological work documents neighborhood disparities in state surveillance. This data visualization expands on this work by mapping uneven patterns in the locations of Flock automated license plate readers (ALPR). I draw on crowdsourced data on the locations of 116,309 Flock ALPR cameras to describe the characteristics of census block groups (CBG) by camera density. These data provide an unprecedented view into the national distribution of police surveillance infrastructure. More than a quarter of Americans live in a CBG with at least one Flock camera. Furthermore, CBGs with more cameras have larger shares of racially minoritized residents. This uneven pattern is strongest in rural areas and largely absent in cities. These findings suggest that racially minoritized residents, particularly those in rural areas, may face disproportionate exposure to this growing network of algorithmic surveillance.

abstract: Formalization is necessary to operation and is the standard remedy after coordination failure: when an event goes badly, the response is almost always more specification. This paper argues that the remedy routinely produces the defect it was meant to cure, because a procedure specified tightly enough to remove discretion cannot be followed in the conditions for which it was most needed. The cost is not the single departure but the standing the instrument loses once it is known to require breaking. A formal structure is tenable when it can be complied with as written across the conditions it governs, including conditions it did not anticipate, without anyone having to breach or override it. Tenability is distinct from flexibility, vagueness, and permissiveness, and is achieved by restricting what an instrument claims rather than by adding to it. Seven drafting devices accomplish that restriction: scope restriction, tiered normativity, anchored discretion, burden allocation, precedence rules, guidance by worked example, and temporal and successional scoping. The paper treats these as alternative routes to one property rather than a checklist, illustrated from statute, case law, and municipal and federal practice, including a 2025 decision voiding a municipal agreement drafted so that it had to be broken. The contribution is conceptual: a name, a diagnostic test applicable to any existing instrument, a repair inventory pairing each device with the failure it forestalls, and a reframing of policy review from what an instrument omits to what can no longer be followed. Existing work names the tension between rules and practice but takes the drafting as given.

abstract: Public debate in Türkiye often assumes that society’s values are changing rapidly, whether toward individualism, conservatism, or a break between generations, yet such claims are rarely tested against representative data. This report describes the value priorities of adults in Türkiye using a nationally representative telephone survey conducted in August–September 2026 (n = 993). Values were measured with a twenty-item scale adapted from the Human Values Scale of the twelfth round of the European Social Survey (ESS) and grounded in Schwartz’s refined theory of basic human values. The findings are compared with ESS measurements of Türkiye from 2004 and 2008, with Turkish value studies dating back to the 1970s, with twenty-nine ESS countries, and with the pan-cultural value hierarchy. Differences are evaluated by effect size rather than statistical significance, and shared values are treated as findings in their own right. Values in Türkiye form a tiered structure rather than a strict rank order. Security, Face, Benevolence, Universalism, and Humility are endorsed with high and closely similar importance, with Security and Face at the top. More than 90% of respondents rate protecting nature, a strong state able to protect its citizens, personal safety, and never being humiliated as very important. Conformity, Self-Direction, Tradition, Hedonism, Stimulation, and Achievement form a second, more selectively endorsed cluster. Within Power, wealth is considered important by two thirds of respondents, while exercising control over others is clearly rejected. This profile is shared across social groups. For the most highly valued values, no difference by age, education, gender, or region exceeds a small effect size. Age is the main dividing line, operating through Tradition, Conformity, and Self-Direction, but these differences reflect the intensity with which the same values are held rather than a generational rupture. The core structure has also been stable over time. Security, Benevolence, Universalism, and Tradition form the top cluster in 2004, 2008, and 2026 alike. Compared with other societies, Türkiye shares the common hierarchy in which Benevolence, Universalism, and Security rank highest. What distinguishes it is the relatively high importance of Tradition and Rule Conformity and the relatively low importance of Self-Direction. Read together with classic analyses of state and society in Türkiye, the findings suggest that expectations of a protective state and an ethic of solidarity rooted in close relationships have broad counterparts at the level of individual values, and they set clear limits on common narratives of value change.

abstract: Wisconsin’s conflict over our relationship with the wolf is argued where populations are counted and status is set in law. The middle ground between them — where a person comes to believe what he believes about relationship together with others (psychological and social identity) — is nearly empty in the public record. In four sections this paper treats the conflict over wolves as historical, structural and systemic and offers a scaffold and a method for locating any response to it, based upon the scientific literature and evidence-based programmatic efforts. Procuring a Life describes the declining and recovering population records of four predator and four prey animals — beaver, bison, elk, deer, dog, fox, coyote, wolf — in the terms of the currencies into which each was placed by those who effectively exerted control over what happened to those populations. Processing into Provision or Product defines a currency as the form into which an animal’s life is converted — food and clothing, fur, money, symbol and knowledge — and then follows the animal through nine conversions by human hands. From provision to sign, the passage of one skin, a mink coat, is followed through every hand that held it. Causes and Consequences of Conversion names the four hands at every conversion — producer, promoter, arbitrator, processor of currency and value— and finds four regularities in the passage: value rises with each hand; distance from the source and repeated conversion in form increasingly disconnects the handler from relationship with the animal; cost and benefit accrue unequally; and return to original sources has no reliable mechanism of its own. This accounting is contrasted with the value the living wolf produces that no hand holds: fewer deer–vehicle collisions and a richer understory, absent from the conflict because few keep an accounting of them. Mapping Layers characterizes five relevant systemic levels, and finds the critical two middle layers — psycho-social identity development and small-group formation — without survey, study or program. In the one Washburn County district followed class by class, the boys stand above the state in language at grade 8 and at the state at grade 11 — the years in which hunting is learned — a loss the structure of the households does not predict and the paper reads as made in the sparse-language groups, the team and then the camp, whose standards a few leaders set. The review of the literature distinguishes the ecologists’ attitude surveys from a developmental psychologist’s study of motivation still to be done, compares a scaffold of women’s intergenerational return of relationship beside the market chain that skims off value at each phase of conversion, and closes with PACKS, a five-year family-based research methodology and program designed to fill the gap in conceiving ways to resolve our conflicts around wolves and other wild animals.

abstract: Urban environments are facing growing ecological and social pressures associated with Urban commons initiatives potential to contribute to broader urban transformations may remain limited without institutional recognition. This study examines the mechanisms through which partnerships between municipalities and UCIs, termed as public-commons partnerships (PCPs), form around the governance of land-related urban resources. Drawing on 24 semi-structured interviews and 118 questionnaire responses from UCI representatives in Switzerland, we identify four categories of PCPs: enduring and mutual-recognition-based partnership, sustained yet non-dependent partnership, temporary and conditional partnership, and limited or absent partnership. Partnerships emerge when UCIs align with municipal objectives by advancing policy goals, resonating with political priorities, or strengthening policy implementation by same time, municipalities mobilize publicly owned land through diverse property-right institutional recognition and visibility while promoting urban resource governance that prioritizes collective use value, solidarity, and ecological stewardship. We argue that authorities mobilize public resources and regulatory capacities, while commons organizations contribute grassroots innovation, collective self-governance, and social more inclusive and ecologically oriented governance on urban environments.

abstract: Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet — and across numerous measurement techniques — more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

abstract: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lack systematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

abstract: Trials of recovery training report mean gains in psychological detachment, but the mean does not show whether training helped the employees who detached least or those who already detached well. An aptitude-treatment account predicts larger gains at the low end of the baseline distribution (compensation), and a cumulative-advantage account predicts larger gains at the high end (accumulation). I tested the two accounts in a prespecified reanalysis of a randomized trial among German employees (N = 393, 76% women, mean age 41; 247 with posttest data) that compared a wait-list control with a 6-week cognitive-behavioral recovery training and a 6-week mindfulness-based training. The primary test was the baseline × condition interaction in a Lin-adjusted regression of posttest detachment; secondary analyses were quantile treatment effects, changes-in-changes and Lee bounds, multiple imputation, and a missingness model. Both trainings raised detachment at the mean baseline by about 0.9 points, and quantile effects were larger at the .25 than at the .75 quantile in both groups. The cognitive-behavioral interaction was −0.21 (95% CI [−0.50, 0.08]), leaning toward compensation, and the mindfulness interaction 0.04 (95% CI [−0.24, 0.33]); the condition contrast was 0.25 (95% CI [−0.01, 0.51]), and all three intervals included zero. Dropout before the posttest was not detectably patterned by baseline detachment in any group. The results support neither compensation nor accumulation. Neither training detectably favored employees at either end of the baseline distribution, and the intervals bound how large either pattern could be in a trial of this size.
